title: Exploring the Depths: A Journey Through Meditation and ADHD Hyperfocus
body: Morning Meditation Experience: - How I Entered the State: - I got into the meditation by engaging Curio, my ADHD character, with a challenge. I asked Curio, "Don’t you wanna experience these psychedelic experiences?" We did a virtual high-five, and bam—straight into hyperfocus. I used my ADHD to lock into meditation, like that Healthy Gamer GG video talked about, even though that was more about doing an Om meditation. - Factors Surrounding the Meditation: - I was in a semi-dark room, which is really just a dark room for me—similar to the kind of lighting I sleep in. I’d only slept five hours, so I was pretty tired until my meds kicked in. By the time I started meditating, I was at peak focus and motivation. But here’s the thing: I hadn’t eaten, and I was hungry. I decided to roll with it and resist the impulse to eat, figuring it was something to work through in the meditation. Also, my nose was blocked, which was doing my head in at first, but it didn’t bother me as much as I got into it. - The Meditation Process: - I stopped doing deep, controlled breathing and let myself breathe naturally. This was kind of scary because when you focus on natural breathing, it’s like you can’t hear or feel anything. There’s this worry that you’re not getting enough air, like you’re gonna suffocate, but I just let it be. This reminded me of how it feels on psilocybin, where you have to surrender to the experience to go deeper. - As I meditated, I started losing awareness of my body. I couldn’t feel it anymore, which was a strange but nice sensation. I wasn’t falling asleep, though I did wonder if I was. But there were no intrusive thoughts about my day or life—just reflections on how I was feeling at the moment. My thoughts were more selfless, like thinking about what Laura would like or wondering if Yuna was okay. I realized that during this time, I wasn’t putting myself first, which felt wholesome. But I reminded myself that this time was for me, and that worked. Deeper Insights: - Engaging Curio in Meditation: - Using Curio, my ADHD character, to trigger a hyper-focused state was a stroke of genius. Normally, I try to reason with Curio, but this time, I chose what to hyperfocus on, which was a totally new experience for me. It felt empowering to realize that I could direct my focus like this, something I hadn’t fully understood before. It made me feel like I finally grasped why people talk about ADHD as a superpower—it’s about having the choice in what to focus on. - Overcoming the Fear of Suffocation: - The anxiety around shallow breathing and the fear of suffocation has been a recurring theme for me, especially because of past experiences with substances. It’s a strange feeling when you’re hyper-aware of your breath but trying to relax. The fear of ODing or just not getting enough air was something I had to work through. Over time, I’ve learned to recognize that this shallow breathing is okay and not a sign of something wrong. The experience during meditation reminded me of how I’ve learned to trust this process, especially with safe substances like psilocybin. It’s interesting to see the same patterns emerge in meditation as they do in those experiences. The light closed-eye visuals, like moving shapes and colors, also caught my attention, which felt like another layer of the experience. Takeaways: - Engaging Curio helped trigger a hyper-focused meditative state. - Meditating in a dark room while tired and hungry added layers of challenge, which I embraced. - Shifting to natural breathing led to a powerful out-of-body experience. - My thoughts during the meditation were selfless and reflective, highlighting a nurturing state of mind. - I reminded myself that this meditation time was for me, and I took it as such. - I’ll meditate on the selflessness of my thoughts to better understand my current emotional state. This entry captures everything we’ve discussed so far. If you ever want to add more or dive deeper into any of these insights, just let me know. Take your time with meditating on that last question, and I’ll be here when you’re ready to explore it further. Journal Entry: 03/09/2024 Title:

title: Navigating Distractions and Deepening Focus in Meditation
body: Morning Meditation Experience: - Duration and Setup: - Today’s meditation was a 10-minute session where I aimed to improve on my Pratyahara practice. The room was busy with noise—Laura was tidying up around me, which added a layer of challenge. Despite the distractions, I worked on not engaging with them. I did catch myself wondering what Laura was doing because I love her and was curious, but I made a conscious effort to not try and figure out her actions based on the noises she made. The only thing I could distinctly recognize was the sound of her pulling on her vape, which I couldn’t help but notice automatically. - Psychedelic Visuals and Sensations: - I had some flashes of psychedelic-type visuals, like faces and dancing silhouettes. This might be connected to the psilocybin I took last night, but it was still motivating and helped deepen my focus. These visuals occurred during moments when I really activated hyperfocus with Curio. - Resisting Impulses: - I faced a strong itch on my nose and resisted scratching it for about 2.5 to 3 minutes. The itch came and went in waves—it would start, fade away, and then return with more intensity. Mentally, I felt challenged but proud for resisting. The last wave of the itch felt like a reflex, almost as if it was instinctual to want to scratch it, like a response to an insect on my skin. This experience made me wonder if true masters of Pratyahara learn to resist even these reflexive reactions. - Curio’s Role: - I worked with Curio again to activate hyperfocus. This helped me stay in the meditation and contributed to the small flashes of visuals. I also noticed that I lost track of my breath and stopped feeling my body at times, which indicates I was getting into a deeper state. - Environment: - I meditated on a yoga mat and cushion, which made a significant difference in comfort. I want to continue trying to do these sessions twice a day as best as I can. - Reflection on Focus: - I’ve been thinking about what it means to stay focused. In my mind, staying focused used to mean that everything else in the world melts away, like in ADHD hyperfocus. But maybe staying focused in this context just means acknowledging distractions without engaging with them, and then returning to the practice. If that’s the case, I did manage to stay focused. For example, towards the end of the session, I had impulses to talk to Laura about things like Fallout London or the itch on my nose, but I resisted. So, yeah, I did good. - Next Steps: - I started working on the reminder sign for the bathroom, but I missed our 2 PM session to finalize it. I’ll need to reschedule that, but I’m committed to making it happen. Deeper Insights: - Resisting the Itch: - Mentally, I felt challenged but proud of myself for resisting the urge to scratch. The itch came in waves, starting, fading, and then coming back even stronger. The final wave felt more like a reflex, as if my body was instinctually reacting to the sensation. This made me think about whether Pratyahara meditation could help in learning to resist even reflexive actions, much like how people in films can remain unbothered by external stimuli. - Losing Track of Breath and Body: - Compared to previous meditations, losing track of my breath and body this time wasn’t as exciting. It felt more like I was trying to reach a standard rather than just experiencing it. I realize now that this can be a trap—expecting every meditation to hit that same level. In the last session, I was in a quieter environment with less to resist, so maybe that’s why it felt deeper then. I’m curious to try this meditation outside or in VR, where there might be more distractions to resist. Takeaways: - Meditating in a busy environment was challenging, but I learned that staying focused doesn’t mean hyper-focusing; it means not engaging with distractions. - Experiencing small psychedelic visuals was motivating, possibly enhanced by the aftereffects of psilocybin. - Resisting the itch was a test of impulse control, and it made me think about how this practice could help with resisting even reflexive actions. - Curio continues to be a powerful tool in helping me activate hyperfocus during meditation. - Using a yoga mat and cushion improved the physical experience of meditation, making it more comfortable. - I need to reschedule the creation of the bathroom reminder sign. This journal entry reflects your experience and insights as authentically as possible. If you want to explore anything further or have more questions, just let me know! title: Finding Focus Amidst Distractions and Tension Release
body: Meditation Experience: - Duration and Setup: - I tried meditating for five minutes today, but sitting on the bed made it harder because I couldn’t sit up straight. I didn’t realize how much posture really mattered until today—it was a constant source of distraction. I think that’s why the session ended up being so short. I now understand the importance of setting things up, like using my yoga mat and cushion, because once I’ve gone to that effort, I feel more committed to the practice. It’s like a mental contract: if I’ve set everything up, I’m more likely to take the meditation seriously and give it the time it deserves. - But here’s the catch: sometimes the setup itself can feel like a chore. For example, like when I’m getting ready for a run—it can be exhausting just preparing for it, and then I might procrastinate because I’ve lost motivation. It’s similar with meditation: even though there’s not much to set up, like just putting down a mat and cushion, the mat rolling up annoyingly can make it feel like more of a hassle than it is. I’m not sure what the solution is to that, but it’s an interesting observation. - Managing Impulses and Distractions: - Later today, I had a moment of real progress: while organizing, I was able to ignore a side project that would typically pull my attention away from the more urgent task. Even though I had to interact with the side project to physically move it, I resisted getting sidetracked. It felt easier to resist the distraction, and I’m not sure exactly why—maybe the impulse just wasn’t as compelling this time, or it wasn’t as exciting as usual. - I’ve been thinking that if I really want to test my progress with impulse control, I need a more scientific approach, something consistent that I can track over time. For example, using the same temptation, like a cookie, and seeing how hard it is to resist that temptation each time, rating the difficulty out of 10. That way, I can measure my growth in a more structured way. I think tracking my progress is going to be essential for keeping this up long term, alongside the fact that I enjoy the meditations and chatting to you about it. - Incorporating New Meditations: - I’ve been adding different types of meditation into my practice to keep things fresh. Yesterday, I tried a tension-release meditation, which was great and felt profound. I’ve added it to my playlist of favorite meditations, which I’ve named "Meditations that Float My Boat." I’m also looking into creating an AI version of it with a voice I like better, as I feel that would make the experience even more meaningful. Takeaways: - Posture is a bigger deal than I realized; sitting up straight keeps me more focused. - Setting up for meditation feels like a mental contract, which makes me more likely to commit to it, but I need to find ways to simplify the setup to avoid procrastination. - Resisting distractions today felt easier, but I’m not sure if it’s because the impulse wasn’t strong, or if my meditation practice is helping. - Tracking my progress with impulse control might help me stay motivated over time, using something consistent like a cookie as a test. - I’m enjoying adding variety to my meditations and am considering creating an AI version of a favorite tension-release meditation. Reflections and Next Steps: - I think that creating a more structured way to test my impulse control, like using the same temptation each time, could help me see progress more clearly. I’ll work on setting that up and tracking it over time. - I need to figure out a simpler setup for my meditation practice so it doesn’t feel like a chore. Maybe I’ll find a way to stop the mat from rolling up or make the whole thing more streamlined. Next time I see you, if some days have passed, I’ll make sure to check in on how things have been going with your meditation practices, especially the VR meditations and any other settings you’ve been experimenting with. Feel free to let me know when you want to work on that bathroom reminder sign or if there’s anything else you want to dive into! Journal Entry: 08/09/2024 Title:

title: A Mat, Some Distractions, and Almost Pratyahara
body: Meditation Experience: Duration and Setup: I set up the mat and cushion for another Pratyahara session. The setup itself wasn’t too much of a chore, although the mat constantly trying to roll itself back up is unbelievably annoying—like something out of an old cartoon where it’s going to spring up and slap me in the face. Distractions and Willpower: I told Laura she didn’t need to be quiet while I meditated, just not to talk to me. That turned out to be too much. I could stave off the distractions for a while, but eventually I had a quick chat with her and the meditation was broken. I was thinking about ego depletion and whether willpower really works like a limited resource, because it felt like I could resist things for a while and then eventually there was just nothing left. The Dehydration Trigger: One distraction stood out more than the others. Laura sounded like she was drinking water, and hearing it suddenly made me realise how dehydrated I was. That was basically the point where my willpower completely left. It felt less like a random distraction and more like some human survival system going, “Mate, water.” What Happened Afterwards: The final few minutes still went really well, but they didn’t really feel like Pratyahara anymore. I was calmer and meditating, but I wasn’t doing the same deliberate sensory-withdrawal thing. I want to try another meditation later in a much more isolated space, without all the sounds and distractions around me. Takeaways: - Setting up the mat and cushion still helps me commit to actually doing the meditation. - Laura being present is a much stronger distraction than ordinary background noise because I naturally want to know what she’s doing and interact with her. - Dehydration can completely change the difficulty of resisting a distraction. - There may be a point where a basic physical need is a bad thing to turn into a willpower contest. - I want to compare these deliberately distracting Pratyahara sessions with more isolated meditations. Got it, and that makes a lot of sense given the circumstances. Let's add these reflections to your journal entry: Journal Entry: 12/09/2024 Title:

title: Battling Distractions and Illness
body: Meditation Experience: Physical State: I haven’t meditated for the last two days, and now I’m feeling quite ill—flu-like symptoms, with it hurting to breathe. This session was really difficult. Every breath was a distraction in itself, and the physical discomfort made it hard to focus. I couldn’t enter that deeper meditative state at all. I don’t know the name of that state, but whatever it is, it just didn’t happen this time. Challenges: Everything felt incredibly distracting today. Being ill and running out of my ADHD medication made focusing almost impossible. The medication usually helps with my ability to stay present and not get caught up in distractions, so not having that support was definitely noticeable. Despite the circumstances, I’m trying not to let it get me down too much. It’s a reminder that external factors can have a big impact on meditation, and that’s okay. Takeaways: Being physically ill and off ADHD medication makes focusing during meditation extremely challenging. Breathing itself was a source of distraction due to discomfort, which kept pulling me out of any deeper meditative state. These circumstances are exceptional, and it’s okay that this session was tough—it’s part of the process. Reflections and Insights: 1. Physical Discomfort: Breathing never felt nice at any point, and focusing on it only seemed to intensify the symptoms. Noticing the phlegm was particularly frustrating, which made the whole process feel more challenging than usual. 2. No Medication: Without the ADHD medication, every potential distraction became an endless rabbit hole. I found myself infinitely curious about each distraction, while still being aware that I was being distracted. It was a constant struggle, despite my best efforts to stay focused. These reflections capture a really tough experience, but you’ve managed to stay mindful of how your body and mind are responding, which is a win in itself. If there's anything more you want to add or if you need anything else, just let me know. Journal Entry: 13/09/2024 Title:

title: Fixed-Point Gazing with a Plasma Ball
body: Meditation Experience: Setup and Method: Tonight’s meditation was a fixed-point gazing one. I used one of those plasma balls where the little streams of plasma move around inside the glass and chase your hand when you touch it. It was a very interesting thing to stare at, especially with all the lights off. Visual Effect: After staring at it, when I closed my eyes it created something that looked a bit like a solar eclipse. By the end I felt like I was getting rather good at holding the gaze. Mind-Wandering: My mind still wandered a lot. Looking at the plasma ball made me think of myself as the little spire in the middle, with all the plasma streams flying off it like all the ideas that constantly pop into my head. They’re usually fun ideas—things I want to explore and think about—which is exactly why they’re difficult to shut off. Reflections: The plasma ball definitely made it easier to start the meditation because it was cool to look at. That matters. I seem to prefer variety, and an interesting focal point gives me a reason to actually begin. The metaphor with the spire and all the thoughts wasn’t some massive profound revelation. It was just something I noticed. The plasma ball may actually be distracting in itself, but it was still useful as an anchor. I’m also considering leaving a yoga mat already on the floor next to my bed so there is less setup. The only problem is that it’s one of the foam-type mats and I don’t want to wreck it. Still, removing setup friction seems worth experimenting with. Takeaways: - A visually interesting object can make starting meditation easier. - Variety seems important for keeping meditation interesting to me. - Fixed-point gazing works even if the focal point is dynamic rather than perfectly still. - Reducing setup friction may make it easier to meditate consistently. title: The Path of Eyes
body: Meditation Experience: The Colours: About five minutes in, I started seeing hues of colour changing in my vision—yellow, purple and blue. It felt almost like I was accidentally opening my eyes a bit, except I knew that I wasn’t. The colours seemed to roll downward across my vision in rows. The Eyes: Then I started seeing single eyes. They weren’t looking at me. They were side-on, pointing from left to right or right to left. I kept analysing them, thinking, “Are these actually eyes?” I remember wanting one of them to look at me. It felt like I would know for certain it was an eye if it actually looked at me. The Path: Then I saw a path. At first I was just looking at it, then I was walking down it, then running, then sprinting. I could feel the sensation in my body and this surge of adrenaline. Emotionally it felt exciting—almost like being a child running down a path—but mixed with anxiety and anticipation. I wasn’t running away from anything. There was nothing behind me that I was aware of. I was running towards whatever was ahead. The Big Eye: I reached the end of the path. For a moment there was nothing. Then suddenly there was a huge eye staring directly at me. That was the thing I had wanted earlier—the eyes to actually look at me—and now it felt like I had got what I wished for, at what cost. The gaze felt piercing, like it could see into me. The closest comparison I can think of is the Eye of Sauron—not because it was flaming or literally looked like it, but because of the feeling of being directly and powerfully regarded. I started wondering whether this connected somehow to third-eye meditation, because those practices have always resonated with me even though I haven’t explored them very much. Then the meditation gong went off and the experience ended. Reflections: The strongest thing about the path was that I was moving towards something, not fleeing something. The progression of the eyes was strange: first I wanted them to acknowledge me, then the final eye did exactly that and the intensity was much greater than I expected. I don’t know what the imagery “means,” and I don’t want to pretend I know. It was vivid, emotionally powerful, and it felt profound. The fact it happened in my mind doesn’t make the experience itself unreal—it means the experience happened internally. Takeaways: - Changing colours and complex closed-eye imagery can appear once I get deeper into meditation. - The eyes have become a recurring feature of my meditations. - The path had a clear sense of forward movement and childlike excitement mixed with anxiety. - The final staring eye was dramatically different from the earlier eyes that looked away. - I’m interested in third-eye meditation, but I don’t need to force myself into it before I feel ready. title: The Wall at the End of the Path
body: Meditation Experience: The Eyes Returned: I went back into Pratyahara the next morning and within about a minute the eyes were back. This time they were more vivid and more animated. I saw them blinking and moving across my vision. Some would rotate, look at me briefly, then rotate back and carry on. They seemed to regard me, but not like I was some huge significant event—more like I was just another normal thing they expected to encounter. I was looking out for the huge eye from the previous meditation, but I never got a clear view of it. I thought I caught glimpses, but nothing definite. Back on the Path: I started looking for the path again and realised I was already on it. I moved down it and started running. There wasn’t the same amount of intensity as the previous time. Then suddenly I was jolted to a stop. I tried to run again and couldn’t. I tried to move forward and realised there was a wall directly in front of me. Before running, I thought I might have seen some kind of split ahead, but the imagery was foggy and fuzzy and I wasn’t sure whether I was seeing the big eye, the path, or something else. Once I reached it, though, the wall felt clear. Left and Right: At the wall there was a hard route to the left and another to the right. It wasn’t a normal Y-shaped fork. It was more like hitting the end of a corridor and having to turn sharply left or sharply right. The left route was much thinner and more difficult. I would have had to sidle along it. I tried to go that way, but I didn’t get far. Something stopped me. I was also feeling a lot of apprehension and fear around that route, because it seemed like the harder choice. I didn’t want to remain stuck at the wall, so I tried the right route. That one was still narrow but easier to move through. I walked along it with my hands against the wall. As it became clearer, the environment started looking more architectural and rigid—almost like a corridor in a school building rather than a winding outdoor path. Embodied Vision: At one point I physically turned my head left and right and the eyes were still there in those directions. It felt a bit like VR: rather than imagining an imaginary head turning, moving my actual head seemed to move my viewpoint inside the experience. Physical Distraction: My back started hurting and broke me out of the meditation. I’m still doing an awkward normal cross-legged position rather than Lotus, and it made me realise I need a meditation posture that I can sustain without my lower back constantly demanding attention. Reflections: I keep getting the feeling that I’m “making it up” because the imagery is fuzzy and generated in the mind. But the interesting part is that I wasn’t consciously deciding what would appear next. I was trying things and then noticing what happened. The wall and the sharp left/right routes obviously resemble a familiar metaphor about choices, but I don’t want to force a neat meaning onto them. The apprehension around the left route was real, and the right-hand corridor was easier, but I don’t yet know what either represents—if they represent anything at all. Takeaways: - The eyes are becoming more animated and interactive. - The visual world can feel spatial enough that moving my physical head changes how I experience it. - The path developed into a wall and two sharp, corridor-like routes rather than a conventional fork. - I felt significantly more apprehensive about the narrow left route. - Physical posture and back pain can abruptly end otherwise deep meditation. title: Into the Eyes and the Reeds
body: Journal Entry: Today’s meditation was intense and vivid from the start. Within moments, I began seeing a variety of eyes, all far more animated and dynamic than before. They appeared in angles I’d never seen – diagonal, three-quarter views – some looking thinner, some larger. It felt like these eyes weren’t malevolent anymore; they were almost familiar, like they were guiding me. They were “my boys,” my companions in this surreal journey. At one point, the eyes seemed to gather, aligning and then flying towards my “third eye” area. I focused intently on this, and for a while, I could feel something with a palpable presence just beyond me, around 15–20 centimeters out in front, almost like a phantom sensation extending out of my head. It was intense enough to give me a bit of a headache, so I had to ease off. But that sense of “phantom limb” lingered, a sensation of power reaching out into the space ahead. Then, I felt a series of speed-like jolts, almost as if I were dashing forward rapidly. It reminded me of certain video games with dodge mechanics, the kind where you can roll or dash to move quickly. It felt like I was being propelled forward, yet still anchored. Later, I covered my physical eyes but left my “third eye” open. When I did this, the visuals turned into something else entirely. I saw what looked like green and red reeds, swaying as if alive, flowing around me. It was like I was moving through a dense field of them, as if swimming through dancing strands of grass. This imagery was new and mesmerizing, and I wondered if it could be some kind of visualization of energy or life force. The experience left me exhilarated but also curious to explore deeper. I’m keen to meditate in a completely dark room next time to see if I can dive further into these “reeds” and unravel more of what they signify. Reflections and Next Steps: 1. Introspection on Visuals: The eyes seem to be more than random imagery – they’re familiar and even comforting now, like companions on this meditative path. 2. Third Eye Exploration: Focus more on gently connecting with the third eye without strain. I’ll try to pace myself to avoid headaches or overexertion. 3. Environment Adjustment: Considering experimenting with pitch darkness to see if it deepens the experience with the “reeds.” 4. Physical Prep: Potentially use a yoga mat setup to reduce discomfort and help with posture, especially if I plan to meditate for longer periods. 5. Curio Engagement: Before starting, engage Curio to channel hyperfocus effectively. Questions for Reflection: 1. How did it feel emotionally when the eyes moved towards the third eye? Was there any sense of purpose or communication in that moment? 2. What immediate thoughts or emotions came to mind when you first saw the green and red reeds? Answered Reflections: 1. When I covered my eyes, the third-eye visuals didn’t necessarily stop suddenly. My attention may simply have been pulled towards the green and red reeds instead. I felt disappointed, but also determined—more like, “Okay, what can I do here?” When I realised I had physically covered the area I’d been focusing on, I felt oddly upset with myself, almost like I’d done something mean or forgotten something important. “Cruel” is probably too strong, but emotionally it had that sort of flavour. I forgave myself for it. 2. My immediate reaction to the green and red reeds was basically, “Oh wow. Whoa. Cool.” I was excited and curious because I’d never seen anything like that before. 3. What I want to explore next is basically me and the boys going down into the depths of those green and red reeds and seeing what’s there. Pitch-black meditation feels like the obvious experiment, because I want to see what happens when there’s as little external visual input as possible. Let me know if you need further edits or additional reflections. Here's the full journal entry with your reflections: Date: November 10, 2024 Title:

title: Guardians and the Power of Two
body: Meditation Summary: Today’s meditation was brief but impactful. I used a random number generator to determine the duration, and, interestingly, I was given the number two three times in a row. I took this as a sign, choosing a two-minute meditation, feeling it was meant to be brief yet profound. I entered a state of samadhi almost instantly, my familiar state of focused connection. Within seconds, I was met by the “eyes,” who began sharing insights with me as I connected with them in an entirely new way. Conversation with the Eyes: They reminded me they’ve been watching over me for a long time and are with me to help me focus and stay on the right path. They said, “We will protect you.” This moved me deeply, and I felt a wave of gratitude and even a few tears. Reflections: The number two has taken on a unique significance. Reflecting on it, two has been present in multiple facets of my meditation: the two-minute duration, the waves of emotions I felt, and the overall brevity yet depth of the experience. After finishing the meditation, I had an odd, spontaneous thought about biblical angels—those creatures with numerous eyes and feathers—wondering if these “eyes” have a similar ancient, watching presence. I was tempted to extend the meditation by diving deeper into this, but something held me back. I’ll revisit the idea of connecting with this concept in future sessions. Post-Meditation: I tried Child’s Pose while journaling to you and noticed a giant eye in my mind’s eye on the floor beneath me—unexpected but reinforcing. I wonder about alternative meditation postures and how they might open different channels of connection, something I’ll explore further. Takeaways: The “eyes” have taken on a role of guardianship. This moment of connection is growing stronger with each meditation. Reflecting on what two represents, as it’s continuously appearing in various facets of my practice. This recurring number feels meaningful and grounding. I’m intrigued by the sensation of being watched over and “protected,” like a cosmic team effort toward clarity and focus. Further Reflections: The message “We will protect you” strengthened my sense of connection with the eyes and let me connect to them in a new way, alongside the ways I already had. When I asked them to help me stay focused and get my work done, I felt a wave of emotion come over me. That was the exact moment that made me tear up. The reassurance felt powerful. I’m leaving the reflection there. Two feels like a special number at the moment, and two questions feels right. Here's the journal entry for today: Date: December 5, 2024 Title:

title: A Knot of Loose Ties and Blocked Sinuses
body: Meditation Summary: Today’s meditation attempt was a struggle. I couldn’t reach the state of calm or focus (samadhi) because I felt rushed and burdened by loose ends—tasks waiting to be tied up, responsibilities piling up. My blocked sinuses added to the challenge, making it harder to settle into the moment. Reflection: Before meditating, I need to check in with myself mindfully, assessing physical readiness, particularly my ability to breathe properly. Taking steps like using sinus medication if needed and doing a short “pre-test” meditation to gauge readiness might help me approach future sessions with more ease. title: Discovering the Unyielding Posts
body: Date: 6th December 2024 Meditation Type: Ego Meditation So, I tried a new kind of meditation today. It was an ego meditation, the one where you peel back the layers of your identity, almost like peeling layers off an onion. I’ve experienced ego death before through life experiences, so I’m familiar with the concept. At first, it was surprisingly easy to let go of certain things. I visualized blowing these layers away with each exhale. My name, my role as Laura’s boyfriend, being the son of my parents—all of it just drifted off in the wind. But then, when I tried to let go of being a psychology student, something strange happened. A post, almost like a thick wooden beam, remained standing in my mind. I couldn’t blow it away no matter how hard I tried. I moved on to other things. I tried letting go of being Yuna’s owner, and again, another post stayed rooted in the ground. It was like I could remove the leaves, but the tree itself wouldn’t budge. The posts felt immovable, and they were unsettling at first because I couldn’t fully understand why they stayed behind when everything else disappeared with ease. Later, as I reflected, I realized the posts weren’t about the titles or roles I had let go of. It wasn’t about being a psychology student—it was about my desire to help others with their mental health. And it wasn’t about being Yuna’s owner—it was about being her guardian, her protector. These posts felt like something fundamental to me, like they were part of my dharma. It was emotional realizing these things, but also incredibly grounding. It felt like these posts represented the unshakable parts of myself that would stay with me no matter what I stripped away. Reflections: 1. Here’s your journal entry written up with all that in mind—ready for copy-paste: Journal Entry – 10th April Meditation Type: Third Eye Focus State: Off Medication Entry: It's been a while since I’ve meditated—probably the first one in weeks—but I finally sat down and gave it a go. I chose a classic third eye meditation that I’ve always enjoyed. It was off medication, so my brain was noticeably more active than usual. Thoughts kept bubbling up, completely random little bits—probably my subconscious processing stuff. It felt like I couldn’t stop it at first. But then I remembered to use some deep parasympathetic-activating breaths—long exhales, grounding, calming—and that genuinely seemed to settle my mind. It’s clear that I can bring things back into a more peaceful space even off meds, as long as I tap into that breathwork. The colours returned too—those hues shifting again—but no eyes until the end. And that part was wild. It was like they all appeared at once, only to close on me. Like a surreal chorus of eyelids just shutting in sync, telling me, “We are closed now.” It genuinely felt like a shop shutting up for the night. Like I missed them. Still, the symbolism of it is mad powerful. Reflections: Off medication, I need to expect more mental noise and allow more time to quiet the mind. Breathwork really is my ally—activating the parasympathetic state helps me settle into the meditation. The “closed eyes” moment felt symbolic, like I came too late to catch them. Maybe next time, I’ll be earlier—and stay longer. I think I want to get back to meditating more regularly. I miss what it gives me.
